THIS CASE IS NOT CYSTIC FIBROSIS: there are no clinical data on the patient. It serves to learn to recognize bronchiectasis, which is the main finding in cystic fibrosis as well.
CT signs of bronchiectasis: bronchus-to-artery ratio > 1 (signet ring sign), failure of the bronchus to taper toward the periphery, bronchi visible within 1 cm of the pleura. Forms: cylindrical (tubular), varicose (beaded), cystic (clustered). Often thickened walls, mucus plugs, areas of air trapping.
The distribution points to the cause: upper lobes in cystic fibrosis and allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis (central); lower lobes in post-infectious sequelae, aspiration, immunodeficiency, primary ciliary dyskinesia; middle lobe and lingula in nontuberculous mycobacterial infections.
Caution: in the left lower lobe, some of the dilated bronchi lie within atelectatic parenchyma next to the effusion; in collapsed lung the bronchi can appear wider in a reversible way. On the right the dilatations are in aerated lung: there the sign is reliable.
Bronco più largo della sua arteria = bro: Bronchus wider than its artery = bronchiectasis. Upper lobes: think of cystic fibrosis; lower lobes: post-infectious sequelae and aspiration.
